title: The Maya Civilization
summary: Josh and Chuck (with Jerry in the booth) survey the ancient Maya civilization: why they are considered one group despite being many independent city-states, their periods (Pre-Classic, Classic golden age), architecture and astronomy, zero and calendars, the 2012 "end of the world" myth, the creation story from the Popol Vuh, agriculture and water engineering (cisterns, zeolite filtration, terraces, milpa slash-and-burn), the ballgame, the supposed collapse versus dispersal, Spanish colonial book burning and syncretism, the Guatemalan genocide of the 1980s, and human sacrifice (cenotes, isotope study of teeth). Opens with a Too Scary, Didn't Watch plug and ends with a listener mail about kidney donation.

segments.title: Opening plug and banter
segments.summary: Chuck plugs his guest spot on the Too Scary, Didn't Watch podcast reviewing Don't Breathe. Hosts introduce the Maya anthropology edition and note earlier Maya-related episodes, including the Maya calendar and climate and the fall of the Maya.

segments.title: Mayan stereotypes and Apocalypto
segments.summary: Banter about the Mel Gibson film Apocalypto and its violence, followed by the start of myth-dispelling: the Maya still exist today and did not vanish.

segments.title: Maya were not one unified people
segments.summary: The hosts explain that the Maya were dozens of city-states that traded, traded ideas, and warred with each other, sharing a geographic region spanning southern Mexico, Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador and Belize.

segments.title: Pre-Classic period and organic city growth
segments.summary: The Pre-Classic period saw agriculture (maize, beans, squash) and early architecture built over older structures. Cities grew organically rather than from central planning, connected by causeways.

segments.title: Maya population, architecture and construction
segments.summary: Estimates of about forty cities and a population of several million up to fifteen million are discussed. Limestone construction without metal tools or draft animals is described, along with temple orientation aligned to solstices and equinoxes.

segments.title: Hierarchy, warfare and early European discovery
segments.summary: Some city-states had rigid, divine-king hierarchies with priestly classes and ritual sacrifice, while others did not. Early European researchers assumed a peaceful culture until fortresses and warfare evidence and decipherment revealed violence.

segments.title: Olmec influence and priestly astronomy
segments.summary: The Olmec are described as an influence on the Maya and one of six pristine civilizations. The priestly class developed mathematics and astronomy, predicting solar eclipses and tracking Venus, during the Classic period.

segments.title: Maya calendars and the 2012 doomsday myth
segments.summary: The Maya had a 365-day solar calendar with eighteen months of twenty days plus a five-day unlucky period, and a 260-day sacred calendar. The December 2012 end-of-world idea is described as a misreading of the Long Count reset, popularized by the film 2012.

segments.title: Maya creation story and religion
segments.summary: The Popol Vuh and Chilam Balam texts describe creation: wood and reed people, mud people, and finally humans made from maize dough and blood. The Maya pantheon was shared across city-states and traded.

segments.title: Maya agriculture and water engineering
segments.summary: Maya farming techniques are covered: underground cisterns plugged with stucco, aqueducts, zeolite and quartz water filtration at Tikal-area reservoirs, terraced fields, raised beds with aquaculture, and milpa slash-and-burn with fallow cycles.
